title: WEIGHTS vs MACHINES: Which one is better for muscle gains?
summary: NH revisits the free weights vs machines debate, arguing free weights should form the bulk of training but machines have a real role for managing tendon and stabilizer fatigue. He criticises machine-only training for restricting movement, limiting range of motion, being boring, encouraging no progressive overload and junk volume, and keeping novices small.
claims: Early YouTube fitness bodybuilding was machine-dominated; the powerlifting boom flipped the culture so that free weights now win and skipping bench/squat/deadlift is seen as fatal to gains
NH started training with only machines and cables, then switched to only barbells and dumbbells after watching powerlifting content
There is no clear winner between machines and free weights; free weights are probably better for muscle, but machines are not inferior in every respect
Older lifters in their 50s-60s tend to favor machines because they are easier on the joints and because their idols used them

Bronze and silver era bodybuilders built their physiques with barbell compounds; machines arrived later together with subpar programming that shunned compounds and progressive overload, which produces poor natural physiques
Machines are not better just because they are more recent; they are a different way to move weight, not an evolution of free weights
Most people who cite 'stabilizer muscles' to defend free weights cannot explain what they are; stabilizers are small muscles that guide and protect the prime movers and tendons
Strains and overuse pains usually hit the small stabilizer muscles, either from neglect or from overtaxing them
If stabilization were all that mattered we would all train on rings; more stabilization demand is not automatically better and stabilizers must not be overtaxed
Because machines reduce stabilizer recruitment they can give tendons and small structures a rest while still training the big muscle, improving the stimulus-to-fatigue ratio
Tendons must still be loaded regularly: overload them and you get tendinitis, underload them and they atrophy and you risk snapping something
Machines that simply copy a free-weight compound are bad; the best machines rethink the movement pattern with different angles while staying biomechanically efficient

Illustration: a bench press might produce 100 points of fatigue with 60 to muscle and 40 to tendon, while a good chest machine produces 50 with 45 to muscle; sometimes the machine is the better choice
Machine-only training is still a mistake because tendons need to accumulate fatigue to get stronger too
Machines restrict freedom: they lock you into one path and one function of a muscle, whereas free weights let you train all its functions
Machine-only programs made people bad at programming because the machine thinks for them

The Smith machine can be more dangerous than a free squat because the bar cannot shift in the sagittal plane to salvage a bad rep; he knows several lifters who hurt their lower back squatting in the Smith

Most machines cannot be adjusted to your anthropometry, so very short or tall lifters repeat a path that does not fit them, which leads to injury or imbalances; good modern machines let you change arm angles and range of motion
NH stalled on machines because the fixed path gave no way to vary the lift
Most chest press and shoulder press machines have a short range of motion because the handles stop you; free weights allow a deeper stretch, which is better for hypertrophy
Machines are boring; boring exercises get skipped, and unless you do a movement consistently you cannot progress on it
Constantly switching machines resets neurological adaptation and leaves gains on the table
NH programmed a single-arm cable row after deadlifts and ended up doing it about twice a year because it was so dull
Machine users rarely progressively overload: plate-loaded machines always carry 45 lb plates and never small plates, and the same people lift the same weight six months later
Sets of 25 on machines are junk volume that gives a pump but does not build much
Putting chains on a machine press is pointless because hanging chains never unload onto the ground, so there is no accommodating resistance
Machine-only lifters tend to skip legs and ego lift with partial range of motion
Novices are drawn to machines because they feel guided and safe, but those who never move beyond them stay small for years; this is especially common in France
Cables invite ego lifting, e.g. triceps pushdowns done by leaning the torso onto the stack, which is no longer a triceps exercise
On cables and machines people rush or drop the eccentric, which is half the rep and the most important part; free weights force you to control the negative
Novices should start with free-weight compounds to learn to move their body through space; machines, cables and the Smith are tools for advanced lifters who understand hypertrophy
The vast majority of training should be free weights; add a machine that suits your biomechanics after the main free-weight movement to sneak in extra tonnage without taxing tendons
Advanced lifters can use the Smith machine for rows and front squats because balance is taken care of
At home a cable stack can be replaced by elastic bands
If you mostly use machines, rotate grips and machines, because a fixed path concentrates any tendinitis in one spot
Machine users still need to log weights and progress: if you leg press six plates now, use seven in a year
You can still hurt your lower back on the leg press; machines do not prevent mistakes
When using machines, superset them, e.g. tie a band to the machine and do an isolation exercise after the machine compound, instead of sitting on it for four minutes
Machines barely tax the cardiovascular system, especially since most target the upper body; older machine-only lifters should do lower body work for heart health
Older lifters' tendons hurt not because of free weights but because they never use them, leaving their stabilizers weak
